Stated Claim / Post Context:
The government says it will close a beloved D.C. park Sunday. Will a judge step in?

Federal judge Ana Reyes grilled the government on Friday about its plans for East Potomac Park, and indicated she could order it to remain open despite President Trump's renovation wishes.

Actual Article Body:
By

Rachel Treisman

The National Park Service wants to close most of East Potomac Park, far more than just the golf course. The perimeter loop is beloved by runners and cyclists.
                
                    
                    National Park Service
                    
                
                hide caption

Federal judge Ana Reyes grilled the government on Friday about its plans for East Potomac Park, and indicated she could order it to remain open despite President Trump's renovation wishes.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Washington, D.C.'s most beloved parks could close indefinitely on Sunday unless a judge decides to intervene. East Potomac Park is home to the municipal golf course that President Trump wants to redevelop into what he calls a championship-level venue. But at a hearing today, administration lawyers argue that repairs are needed not only to the golf course but to the entire recreational area around it. NPR's Rachel Treisman watched the hearing and joins us now. Hey, Rachel.RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: Hey, Scott.DETROW: Did the judge indicate how she'll rule?TREISMAN: District Judge Ana Reyes sounded like she is likely to take action, but she seemed to be grappling with what exactly she can tell the government to do. The government is arguing it needs to close almost the entire park on Sunday for two main reasons. That's the day the lease expires with the golf course's current operator and because it wants to repair the park's seawall, which has been deteriorating for years. Reyes didn't really seem persuaded by that. The government chose to end its operator lease on November 15, which is the day President Trump has said the park would close. And the government acknowledged it doesn't yet have a plan to repair the seawall or a contract to redevelop the golf course. Reyes suggested she'd rule on Saturday. We'll have to see whether she orders the park to stay open or goes even further and tells the government to keep the golf course open, too.DETROW: You've been listening to this since 10 in the morning. What are some of the main sticking points from today?TREISMAN: Yeah. There was a lot of discussion about how Trump's proposed redesign would change a space that so many people here in D.C. just love. Critics say the scale of the course would make it less accessible for beginners, and it would eliminate the perimeter loop that joggers use every day and also for big races, like the Cherry Blossom 10 miler.
